title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 144
paragraphs: To the envoys from Sparta they made this answer: “That the Lacedaemonians should be afraid we might make a treaty with the barbarian was natural enough — but it seems an unworthy fear in men who know so well the spirit of the Athenians: that there is neither so much gold anywhere on earth, nor any land so excelling in beauty and worth, that we would accept it and enslave Greece by taking the side of the Medes. For many and great are the reasons that prevent us from doing this, even should we desire it: first and greatest, the images and houses of the gods burnt and reduced to ruin, which we must necessarily avenge to the utmost rather than make an agreement with the one who did these deeds; and secondly, the bond of Greek kinship, by which we are of one blood and one speech, our common temples, our common sacrifices, our ways of life which are the same for all — things the Athenians could not justly betray. Be assured, if you were not assured of it before, that so long as one Athenian remains alive, we will never make an agreement with Xerxes. We admire, however, the forethought you showed on our behalf, in that you took thought for us who have had our property destroyed and are willing to support the members of our households; as far as you are concerned, the kindness has been fully performed. We, however, shall endure as we can and not be any trouble to you. Now, therefore, with full conviction that this is so, send out an army as quickly as you can; for, as we conjecture, the barbarian will be here invading our land at no distant time — as soon as he hears of the message sent, that we will do none of the things he wanted from us. Therefore, before he arrives in Attica, it is fitting that you come quickly to our aid in Boeotia.” So the Athenians answered, and the envoys departed back to Sparta.
